newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Excess supply weighing on HK infrastructure IPOs.
newsitem.headline: Excess supply weighing on HK infrastructure IPOs.

text.p: An excess supply of highway infrastructure stocks in Hong Kong is likely to dampen the response to upcoming initial public offerings in the sector, underscoring the need to focus on fundamentals, analysts said.

"The response to flotations of new infrastructure issues is expected to be cold, especially those linked with highways because there are far too many stocks in that sector," said Michael Ng, analyst at ASG Investment Services Ltd.
Anhui Expressway Co is expected to come to the Hong Kong market in coming months with a HK$400 million H-share issue.
The company's sole asset is the 134 kilometre Hening Expressway in China running from Dashushan to Zhouzhuang.
Shenzhen Freeway, controlled by the Shenzhen municipal government, is also expected to raise about HK$1.5 billion in a Hong Kong flotation to fund its highway development projects.

"Infrastructure concept stocks are expected to flood the market," said Patrick Chia, research manager from China Everbright Research. "Apart from the upcoming H-shares, many locally-based companies are also expected to spin-off their infrastructure businesses," he said.
Analysts said the disappointing share price performances of Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd and Road King Infrastructure Ltd would also deter some investors from buying into the sector.
Analysts said investors would be more selective and quality conscious towards the infrastructure-related stocks.
"If the stocks are related to other infrastructure sectors such as shipping or airlines it will be another story," said Ng.
Patrick Cheng, corporate finance director at HSBC Investment Bank Asia Ltd, said he was not worried about the excess supply.
"If the issue is undersubscribed, it might give an indication to the market of an oversupply of stocks in a certain industry or a warning about the issue's quality," he said.
Cheng added this was a trend for Hong Kong-based companies to tap the enormous China market.
"We cannot say it is oversupply but it provides more choice for investors," added Isadora Li, director of Crosby Capital Markets (Asia) Ltd.
Analysts said the response to upcoming new listings would also depend on pricing.
"Pricing is important. If an issue prices at a substantial discount to its NAV (net asset value), it will be attractive," said William Lo, head of China research at Kleinwort Benson.
He said the discount to NAV would be a good way to decide how attractive an issue was because earnings potential was difficult to predict at the pre-listing stage.
Lo said if the highways were built in high-growth areas, earnings potential should be good, making certain stocks attractive. "Their fundamentals and qualities will be the main concern," he said.

Among other highway concerns, Jiangsu Ninghu Highway Co is expected to raise funds in Hong Kong, and Guangzhou Investment Co Ltd plans to spin off its interests in highways and bridges in Southern China.
Blue chip Guangdong Investment Ltd also plans to seek a listing in Hong Kong for its China toll road.
Sichuan Chenyu Highway Co, Zhejiang Hangyong Highway Co and Nanjing Shanghai Highway Shareholding Co are also expected to raise funds in Hong Kong.
Other expected spinoffs by Hong Kong-based companies include Fairyoung Holdings Ltd's China port and related businesses and Ideal Pacific Holdings Ltd's China container terminal business.
Civil engineering group Kumagai Gumi (Hong Kong) Ltd intends to spinoff its 30-percent owned Yangpu industrial zone project on China's Hainan Island.

The next issue to come to market is bus line operator Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings Ltd. It offered 59 million new shares at HK$1.80 and plans to use the proceeds to fund a bus venture in China. The issue was 53.5 times subscribed.

Other expected IPOs in the transport sector are China Eastern Airlines, which is planning a dual listing in Hong Kong and the United States by year's end, and China Southern Airlines, expected to list early next year.
